---
title: Off-policy learning
aliases: ["off-policy"]
importance: 86
---
**Off-policy learning** updates target policy using data generated by different behavior policy. Difference may come from old checkpoint, another model, logged production behavior, or asynchronous weight lag.


Importance sampling can correct expectations with ratio $\pi(a\mid s)/\mu(a\mid s)$ when support and probabilities are reliable. In long language sequences, products become unstable, so systems use token/sequence clipping, trust regions, conservative objectives, or bounded replay.

That single ratio corrects an action distribution at a fixed state; full trajectory expectations can also require products of ratios or a method that handles the changed state distribution. Clipping generally trades unbiasedness for lower variance. Behavior probabilities must describe the sampler that actually generated the actions, including temperature and top-k/top-p filtering; raw unmodified model probabilities may be the wrong denominator. Filtering can remove support that a target policy needs.

Offline and off-policy aren't synonyms. Fixed DPO preference dataset is offline, but DPO isn't simply off-policy policy-gradient estimator. Online async RL can be off-policy because generator lags learner.

## Failure modes

- Behavior-policy metadata missing or wrong.
- Target assigns probability where behavior has no support.
- Long-horizon ratios explode or vanish.
- Stale data rewards behavior current environment no longer supports.
- Numeric/tokenization mismatch masquerades as policy change.

## Example

Learner at policy 133 consumes trajectory sampled by policy 130. Stored old log-probabilities and exact tokens allow ratio measurement, but large drift may still require rejection.

## Why it matters here

Large asynchronous RL stacks naturally create off-policy pressure. Explicit policy versions, correction, clipping, and rejection keep throughput optimization from corrupting learning.
